destination.title: The Traffic Stop Was Over. Then the Dog Arrived.

short27: The stop was already over — the warning written, the papers handed back.
So how did the next seven minutes break the Constitution?
Just after midnight in Nebraska, a K-9 officer pulled over Dennys Rodriguez for drifting onto the shoulder.
He ran the checks, wrote a warning, and handed everything back.
But the officer never said you're free to go.
He held Rodriguez seven to eight more minutes, waited for a second unit, then walked a drug dog around the car.
The dog alerted — after the stop was already finished.
In 2015, six to three, the Supreme Court drew the line.
A stop becomes unlawful, Justice Ginsburg wrote, when it is prolonged beyond the time reasonably required to complete the mission.
Once the traffic work is done, the clock stops — extra time for a dog needs its own reason.
It didn't ban sniffs, and it didn't free him; it sent the case back.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: A stop, she wrote — quoting an earlier case — becomes unlawful when it is "prolonged beyond the time reasonably required to complete the mission." And that is why the government's "it was only a few minutes" argument lost.
No one tells the driver he is free to go.
Just after midnight on March 27, 2012, Dennys Rodriguez was driving a Mercury Mountaineer down a Nebraska highway when it drifted onto the shoulder for a moment, then swung back .
Struble never said, "You're free to go." Instead he asked for something more — permission to walk his dog around the car.
On April 21, 2015, the Supreme Court gave its answer — six votes to three.
It did not ban traffic stops, or order officers to rush, or say the police can never act on a hunch.
And now around time itself — the minutes at the side of a road that no one is entitled to take from you.

shorts.angle: The government argued seven minutes was too slight for the Constitution to count, and the Court refused to measure the intrusion by size at all.
shorts.avoids: The existing Short reports the timing rule and Ginsburg's mission language; this cut is the argument the government lost with, and why size was the wrong question.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: Had the dog walked the car before the warning instead of after it, would anything have changed?

lines.text: Seven minutes. That was the whole argument the government took to the Supreme Court, and it lost.
source_lines: The government's answer was, in essence: what's the harm? It was only seven or eight minutes.

lines.text: Officers should have a little breathing room, it argued. A few extra minutes is such a small thing that the Constitution should not even count it.
source_lines: Officers, it argued, should have a little breathing room, a small buffer to run a dog around a car, especially with a second unit on the way for safety.
A few extra minutes is such a small thing, the government said, that the Constitution shouldn't even count it.

lines.text: Lawyers have a name for that. De minimis. Too slight to notice. And it has real force, because seven minutes is not long.
source_lines: In legal terms, it was "de minimis" — too slight to notice
And that argument has real force. Seven minutes is not long.

lines.text: The Court refused to measure the intrusion by whether it felt big or small. An officer cannot bank the minutes he saves by working fast and then spend them on an unrelated investigation.
source_lines: The Court refused to measure the intrusion by whether it felt big or small.
An officer cannot bank the minutes he saves by working fast and then spend them on an unrelated investigation.

lines.text: A traffic stop is a seizure. For those minutes the government is holding you, justified only by its purpose.
source_lines: A traffic stop, she wrote, is a seizure — for those minutes, the government is holding you — and it is justified only by its purpose.

lines.text: A stop may last as long as its job takes, and no longer. When the traffic tasks are finished, the clock stops.
source_lines: A stop may last as long as its job takes, and no longer
The moment the mission is finished, the clock stops, and holding you any longer needs its own reason

lines.text: Sniffing for drugs has nothing to do with keeping a car safe on the road. It is ordinary crime detection.
source_lines: Sniffing for drugs, the Court noted, has nothing to do with keeping a car safe on the road; it is a different errand entirely — ordinary crime detection, aimed at finding evidence

lines.text: The question was never how long the delay ran. It was whether he had any authority to impose it at all.

shorts.loop_join: L5 says the length of the stop was never the real question, so L1's 'seven minutes' is heard again as an argument about the wrong thing.

shorts.angle: Two justices dissented and argued the majority's timing rule punishes the officer who pauses to call for backup before running the dog.
shorts.avoids: The existing Short gives the six to three count and the majority's rule but never says what the three thought; this cut is the dissent's case that a short careful delay was reasonable.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: Did the officer in fact have independent grounds to keep the driver waiting, which is the question the case was sent back to answer?

lines.text: Three justices thought the driver held on that Nebraska shoulder had no case at all. Their reasoning is worth hearing.
source_lines: The dissenters thought the answer was plainly yes.

lines.text: Justice Clarence Thomas, joined by Justice Samuel Alito, argued the whole encounter, all twenty-nine minutes, was reasonable.
source_lines: Justice Clarence Thomas, joined by Justice Samuel Alito, argued that the whole encounter — all twenty-nine minutes — was reasonable, and that the officer had enough to justify the wait regardless.

lines.text: Alito added that the majority's rule was strangely formal. An officer who paused to call for backup before running the dog would now be penalized for the timing.
source_lines: Alito added that the majority's rule was strangely formal: an officer who paused to call for backup before running the dog — a sensible safety step — would now be penalized for the timing

lines.text: Their point was not that time does not matter. It was that a short, careful delay by a lone officer at midnight was reasonable. Which is the very thing the Fourth Amendment asks.
source_lines: Their point was not that time doesn't matter. It was that a short, careful delay by a lone officer at midnight was reasonable — which is the very thing the Fourth Amendment asks

lines.text: The officer ordered him out of the car to wait by the road, then radioed for a second unit.
source_lines: Because Rodriguez would not consent, Struble ordered him to shut off the engine, step out, and wait by the road.
He radioed for a second officer.

lines.text: The majority did not set Rodriguez free. It left a second door wide open and sent the case back down.
source_lines: And it did not set Rodriguez free
In fact, it left a second door wide open.

lines.text: If the officer had a real, specific reason to suspect something more, holding him for the dog might have been perfectly lawful.
source_lines: If Struble had a real, specific reason to suspect Rodriguez of something beyond the traffic violation — genuine reasonable suspicion — then holding him for the dog might have been perfectly lawful

lines.text: So did the officer really cross a constitutional line by pausing to wait for backup at midnight on an empty road?
